newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Alliance & Leicester H1 profit up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Alliance & Leicester H1 profit up.

text.p: Britain's Alliance & Leicester Building Society on Tuesday reported increased pre-tax profits for the first half of the year and said it was on a sound footing for its planned stock market flotation in 1997.

"I am delighted to be able to announce record pre-tax profit...These results indicate that the Alliance & Leicester has created a solid base for our proposed conversion and flotation," chief executive Peter White said in a statement.

Britain's fourth largest building society, which earlier this year decided to opt for bank status, said pre-tax profit for the period was up 12 percent at 183 million pounds ($284 million) from 163 million pounds the year before.

While its gross mortgage lending was significantly lower at 927 million pounds, from 1,757 million at the end of June 1995, this was offset by a successful customer retention policy which resulted in a low level of mortgage redemptions, it said.
The fall in mortgage lending accompanied by increasing profit mirrors a similar trend at Halifax Building Society, which is also moving towards flotation.

The Alliance was now experiencing "a gentle upward movement" in its mortgage lending business as "some of the more ludicrous deals" offered by competitors had been withdrawn, group finance director Richard Pym told Reuters in an interview.
But the market remained very favourable to the consumer, despite the removal of some of the deals offered.
Pym said prices in the British housing market were beginning to rise gently and this should remove negative equity and increase the level of housing transactions.
The society was on schedule with its conversion plans and would put it to the vote of members, its savers and borrowers, before the end of the year.

Conversion costs had already reached 8.6 million pounds and Pym said the total cost would be around 15 pounds for each of the society's 3.5 million members, with postage costs alone likely to reach 10 million pounds.
But Pym said he could not comment on what members were likely to gain in shares if they approved the conversion plans.
"We will be announcing the scheme later this year," he said.

He would not be drawn on how many of the society's members would cash in their shares on flotation and then withdraw any savings they had deposited with the society in the run up to conversion. In order to vote members had to have opened a share account or taken out a mortgage before December 31, 1995.

The society said net retail savings had grown during the first half of 1996. "Into the second half of the year the Alliance & Leicester has continued to perform better than the average of the top 11 UK building societies," it added.
Provisions for bad or doubtful debts of 5.4 million pounds were, Pym said, lower than those of other lenders.
He said the results were very solid and higlighted the Alliance & Leicester's strong financial foundations and conservative lending policies.
While conversion would give the society greater flexibility to undertake acquistions, Pym said there was nothing in the immediate pipeline.
"Most of the foundations have now been laid down for a successful diversified financial services group," Pym said.

The relatively diversified building society, which can trace its mutual roots back to the 1850s and now has a personal banking division and a money transmission unit, was ranked 11th in a recent league table of relative creditworthiness compiled by Rob Thomas, building societies analyst at UBS Limited.
